extracted.intended_audience: educated lay readers and students of geometry/astronomy (readers of a philosophical/astronomical treatise)
extracted.subtask_description: Geometrical/astronomical methods for computing the Sun's real semidiameter and distance from Earth using measured parallaxes, proportions, and right-line trigonometry, with discussion of observational accuracy and illustrative analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion rule relating parallax and semidiameters
rubrics_metrics.description: As the Angle ACB, or, the Horizontal Parallax of the Sun, is, to The Angle DBC, or the apparent Semidiameter thereof; so is The Earth's Semidiameter AB, to The Sun's real Semidiameter DC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proportion (a Rule of Three) is the central computational relation used to infer the Sun's real semidiameter from measured parallax and apparent semidiameter; the text states the rule applies not only to the Sun but to all heavenly bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use angles in place of sines for convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall use the Angles ACB and DCB in the stead of their Sines, which indeed will be most agreeable to Geometrical Exactness; but because there results no considerable Difference from it, and yet the Calculation is much more convenient, we shall use it as other Astronomers have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the raw angles instead of computing sines is acceptable when the difference is negligible and yields simpler calculations; the choice should be justified by the (small) numerical effect on the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical bodies compare by cubes of semidiameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Spherical Bodies are to each other as the Cubes of their Semidiameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convert semidiameter ratios into relative magnitudes (volumes, 'magnitudes' of globes), cube the ratio of semidiameters. The text repeatedly cubes semidiameter ratios to obtain Sun/Earth magnitude comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallax value critically determines computed size (sensitivity to small angles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different assumed parallaxes (Tycho 3 minutes, Riccioli 30 seconds, Newton 10 seconds, La Hire 6 seconds, Huygens ~8–9 seconds, Flamsteed/Horrox ~12 seconds, Wendelins 15 seconds) lead to widely varying semidiameter and cubic-magnitude results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because semidiameter (and especially cubed magnitude) is highly sensitive to small changes in parallax, accurate parallax measurement is essential; small reductions in parallax produce very large increases in computed size (examples and resulting magnitudes are given in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer modern observational methods/instruments for higher accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ancients could hardly be certain to a Minute in their Observations even with their largest Instruments; the Moderns, by the help of their Telescopes and Micrometers, and proper Pendulum-Clocks, seem to have brought this Science of Astronomy to as great a Perfection as is possible, making observations to a few Seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on modern techniques (telescopes, micrometers, precise timing) that enable measurement to seconds rather than minutes; this improves parallax and semidiameter determinations and reduces error in derived magnitudes/distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer solar parallax via parallaxes of nearer planets (Mars, Venus)
rubrics_metrics.description: If observers measure parallaxes of neighbouring Planets, Mars and Venus, which have parallaxes much greater and more capable of Observation, and thence make their Calculation of the Parallax of the Sun and Planets (the Ratio whereof is better and sufficiently known), they may infer that the Sun's parallax consists of a very few Seconds or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When solar parallax is too small to measure directly, use better-measurable planetary parallaxes and known ratios to deduce the solar parallax; this is recommended as a more capable observational route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right-line trigonometry with Earth's semidiameter as unit to compute distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the Semidiameter of the Earth, AB, be taken for a Unit; the Angle of the Horizontal Parallax of the Sun ACB being likewise known by Observations: Then, since BAC is a Right Angle, the Distance of the Sun from the Earth, or from the Line BC, may be easily found by Right-lin'd Trigonometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the right triangle formed by Earth semidiameter and observed parallax angle to compute the Sun–Earth distance in units of Earth's semidiameter. The text gives worked examples for various assumed parallaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conservative lower-bound assumptions to make robust claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The author argues that even if one does not admit large semidiameter estimates (e.g., La Hire's 160 semidiameters or Newton's larger values), a conservative allowance (e.g., assume Sun is at least 100,000 times the Earth) is reasonable and still demonstrates enormous magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When observational uncertainty remains, adopt conservative parameter choices (e.g., a modest parallax) to derive lower bounds that are still sufficient for the argument. This provides robustness against measurement disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human-scale analogies and multiple methods to illustrate astronomical scales
rubrics_metrics.description: To impress the mind with astronomical distances, the author computes time for a cannon-ball to travel from Earth to Sun, and the time for a ship or animal traveling 50 miles/day; these give multi-year or multi-decade scales which illustrate the Sun's remoteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For exposition and pedagogy, complement formal calculations with intuitive comparisons (travel times for cannon bullets, ships, animals) to help readers grasp otherwise-inconceivable scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for atmospheric refraction and variability when discussing twilight and horizon phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The rays of the Sun, passing from a thinner into a thicker Medium, are refracted and turned aside to produce morning and evening twilights; because air density varies by place and time, the bounds or place of twilight are not certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modelling twilight or horizon observations, include refractive effects and acknowledge variability due to atmospheric density and suspended vapours; do not treat twilight boundaries as fixed geometric points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method applicability: same geometric proportion applies to other heavenly bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: And this Rule does not only obtain with respect to the Sun, but likewise to all other Heavenly Bodies whatsoever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same proportion/trigonometric method (parallax vs apparent semidiameter vs real semidiameter) to compute dimensions of other planets or stars where appropriate observational data exist.
